title: Kisa Gotami and Patacara – Grief, Suffering and the Path Forward
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose explores the stories of two early Buddhist women, Kisagotami and Patakara, who exemplify a path to freedom from suffering and impermanence. Through their experiences, the Buddha reveals that attachment to things we love can lead to even more pain when they are lost, but by embracing impermanence, we can find peace and liberation. By examining these stories, we can gain insights into how to cultivate detachment, resilience, and inner freedom in the face of life's challenges and tragedies.

*Even as a mother at the risk of her life watches over and protects her only child, so with a boundless mind should one cherish all living beings, all living things.*
Five years ago, Noman Tim asked me to consider a woman ancestor for my Shiso studies.
That felt out of range and not appropriate with my white, aged male history, so instead I chose the grass-roof hermitage by [unclear: "Sher Du"].
Comfortable, Chinese, male, and venerable.
I left the female ancestors aside, so many male counterparts to focus on.
Then this spring, Noman suggested we senior students investigate our female ancestors in our Spring Dharma Talks.
I reopened some of the texts I had initially considered when first asked.
So tonight I will briefly investigate Kisagotami, a first-generation wanderer, rough-clothed nun, and then delve more deeply into the life and practice of Patakara.

As a little background, Patakara, along with Upali, who was one of the first ten great disciples of the Buddha, and incidentally a barber by trade and who therefore was put in charge of shaving everyone's head, were recognized by the Buddha as proficient in practice for the rules of monastic life, the Vinaya.
Her exemplary observation and recitation of practice set the stage for our practice today.
I hear her harmony when we chant the refuges, as if we are with the Buddha and his students under a banyan tree in the Ganges floodplain forest.
Like Shariputra and Mahaprajapati, Patakara and Kisagotami were the first generation of followers of the Buddha, face-to-face with the Buddha in their practice.
My first exploration in this investigation was the Theragatha, poems of the first Buddhist women.
These Pali texts were transcribed on palm leaves and collected about 350 years after the Buddha's passing.
In our culture, it's hard to think of a poem in our oral tradition from about 1700, and yet that's what these poems were.
They were carried orally for 350 years until they were finally written down.
These in the Theragatha, those are the poems of the male followers, are now considered part of the canon or basic texts of the early phases of Buddhism, and they're found in the sutras.

As I looked over the scholarly Harvard translations, Marty Weingast, the first free women poems of early Buddhist nuns, and Songs of the Sons and Daughters of Buddha, a contemporary translation by Anne Waldman and Andrew Schelling, I seemed drawn to the stories of Kisagotami and Patakara, stories and teachings that are both based on terrible losses, and which, in the mysteries of how traditions and teachings come forward to us, curiously intertwined, diverge, and form the basis of numerous commentaries and cultural variances from Tibet, China, and regions of India.
Looking into these texts, we find that each culture takes the story and melts it around, takes parts of it, changes it, makes it into its own culture.
And so as you investigate, it's very hard to find a true story.
There's a root there, but things change from place to place and over time.

I claim no scholarly background or expertise in these things, so what I offer you tonight is a momentary scan of some available materials, gleaned from the above sources, the Internet and two primary texts: Wendy Garling's Stars at Dawn, Forgotten Stories of Women in the Buddha's Life, and Alice Collette's deeply researched Lives of Early Buddhist Nuns, Biographies as History.
Our practice spans four cultures and more than 2,500 years.
It's sometimes hard to recall how the women I will focus on tonight lived and practiced their newly found beliefs and the physical hardships they endured.

India at the time of the Buddha was a fiercely patriarchal, hierarchical, and relatively wealthy society, for the lucky ones, but a single woman not owned by or in a relationship with a man or distinguished by some culturally regarded courtesan capacities was considered equal to or less than a prostitute.
Many of the Theragatha poems reflect both the disgust and despair women felt about their lives and their bodies and the utter fear they lived in because of their status.
To be free was also to be vulnerable to rape, abuse, or simply abandonment.
There were no temples, monasteries, or shelters.
Practice took place in the forest, under trees, in crude huts, in the companionship, if fortunate, with other followers of the Buddha or another of the multiple philosophy teachers of the time.
From today's perspective, there was nothing romantic or enticing about walking away from your defined life and becoming a wandering monastic.

But it also speaks to the deep power and attraction of a way of life no longer dependent on desire and material goods, but focused on meditation and a fundamental recognition of the impermanence of all things, including the lives of our loved ones and family.
The familiar story of Kishogatami and the mustard seed, as related by Kanho Kris in her talk in February, has a number of fascinating complexities, among which are totally different stories.
In one, she's a wealthy woman during Siddhartha's time who stands on a high balcony and rejects 500 suitors all dressed in their finest garments in favor of the plainly clothed future Buddha.
In a version of this story, their child is Ananda, who becomes Buddha's [unclear: "dependent scribe.
The port story is a favorite tale"].
In another twist, in some contemporary versions to the canon, she morphs into Patakara.
I will tell that story in a few moments.

Both stories, as you will hear, speak to the mother's intense love of her children, to the universality of grief and death, the undeniable reality of impermanence, and to the power of practice as revealed by the Buddha to each of these two afflicted women.
That in this world of suffering, the world we live in through our human form with all of its sorrows and joys, there is a path that frees us from grieving, aging, suffering, and illness.

So let me begin with a contemporary translation of Kisa Gotami's story as a reminder of this universal tale, evidently transformed into many other cultures' moral tales as well, and as a way to open up the complex story of Patakara.
Kisa Gotari and the Mustard Seed.
*Born into a poor family, Kisa Gotami was named Lean Gotami.
Kisa means lean because of the frailness of her body.
When she married a merchant, they chided her as nobody's daughter.
When she bore her son, they finally paid her some respect.
But sadly, the boy died young just after he started to walk.
Kisa went insane with grief.
A wild thought came to her.
"They'll take my child and expose him."
So she lifted the corpse upon her hip and went from door to door begging, "Give medicine to my child."
"Medicine, crazy woman?
What for?" was the response.
She was out of touch.
Someone finally took pity and sent her to the Buddha.*
*He glimpsed the promise in her and instructed, "Go, go enter the town and collect a little mustard seed from any house where no one has died."
She went from house to house, but at each one someone had died.
The truth dawned.
"This will be the situation in the whole town."
She finally sought a charnel ground to place her dead child and spoke.
"No village law, no city law merely, no law for this clan or for that one alone, for the whole world, for the gods even, all is impermanent.
This is the truth."*
*The Buddha asked, "Gotami, did you collect the mustard seed?"
She answered, "This is the work of the little mustard seed," and requested ordination.
She was proclaimed first among wearers of the rough raiment, also called dust heap robes, salvaged cloth from the charnel grounds from wherever they could be found.
Reflecting later, she sang,*
*Excellent to have wise noble friends.
One should know a few things.
It helps your pain, your dukkha.
But one should understand how pain arises, how it ceases.
The eightfold path, the four noble truths, mark the sorrow, mark how it comes.
Being a woman is painful.
Miserable, sharing a home with hostile wives.
Miserable, giving birth in bitter pain.
Some cut their own throats.
More squeamish women take poison.
I saw it, like others.*
*My husband died, two sons dead, and mother, father, brother cremated on the funeral pyre.
Miserable, a whole family destroyed.
Tears shed for a thousand lifetimes.
Watched my babes' flesh devoured by dogs, jackals, and tigers in the charnel ground.
But I survived, quenched desire.
Saw the teachings as a mirror, held up to show me my crazy mind now healed.
The poison darts extracted from my heart.
All is done and done by me.*
The theory: Kisa Gotami saw herself in the mirror and witnessed these things.
So here, in this final stanza, tales and scriptures start to interfold.
Kisama Gotami's story is classic.
A mother loses her only child and suffers unconscionable grief and sorrow.
But where do these other relatives, brothers, husband, father, and mother, just referenced, where do they come into the story?
This is the other story, the story of Patakara: a tale of loss and suffering so profound it is hard to imagine.
While Kisa Gotami became a mendicant monk, Patakara becomes a paragon of practice.
Here is her tale.
Bear with me, this is hard to hear.
Kisa Gotami was the most beautiful young woman in Saravati, the daughter of a wealthy merchant.
When she was 16, her parents secured her on the top floor of a seven-story tower, surrounded by guards, to keep her from the many interested young men.
In spite of this, she fell in love and seduced a family servant.
When her parents arranged her marriage to a social equal, she and her lover eloped.
She was pregnant at this point.
With a few jewels, they went to a small village many miles away where they farmed and had a small grass hut.
As she was pregnant, she begged her husband over and over again to go with her to visit her parents' house.
But he kept putting her off because he knew that if he got there they would torture him or kill him.
She then decided to go by herself, and her husband found her gone and followed her.
She wouldn't return with him.
But before they arrived at her parents' house, she began to have birth pangs.
So they went back to their house in the village.
She became pregnant again.
Her husband again refused to take her to her parents' home.
She went off again carrying the older child, and the husband followed.
Then an unseasonable thunderstorm struck with incessant rain.
Her birth pangs began, so she asked her husband to find some shelter.
The husband chopped down some saplings to make a crude shelter.
But as he labored, a cobra snake bit him and killed him instantly.
Through the stormy night, she watched for his return, waited for his return, suffering birth pangs, and gave birth to their second son.
Both newborn and firstborn cried through the stormy night, protected by their mother.
In the morning, she found her dead husband and blamed herself for his death.
Distraught, she continued towards her parents' home, only to be confronted by the raging Assiravati River.
Too weak to carry both children through the torrent, she carried the newborn across, put him under some leaves, and went back for the older child.
While midstream, she saw an eagle swoop down and grab the newborn.
The older child heard her cries and thought she was signaling him to come to her.
He was immediately swept away by the current.
Wailing and lamenting, half crazed by the loss in a few hours of her husband and both sons, she continued down the road.
Nearing Assiravati, she met a traveler coming from the city.
When she asked about her family, the traveler refused to answer, but pressured by Patakara, he told her the bad news.
Her parents' house had collapsed in the storm, and even now her mother, father, and brother's bodies were being cremated.
The smoke was visible from the road.
With this last horrific news, she lost her mind, her grief too much to bear.
She tore off her clothes, wandered around weeping and wailing, not knowing what she was doing or where she was going.
Everywhere, people pelted her with stones and rubbish and chased her out of the way, a crazy, ostracized, naked woman running around Assiravati.
They called her Patakara, or cloth wanderer, for she wandered without a cloth for protection.
She wandered this way naked and mad for many days until she encountered the Buddha's gathering at the Jeta Grove.
The Dhammapada commentary credits the Buddha's omniscience, revealing that in her past life during the time of Padamuttata Buddha, she had resolved to become a nun well-versed in the law.
The Buddha's disciples tried to protect him from this mad woman, but instead he welcomed her.
Different accounts have him offering various counsel.
"Sister, regain your senses."
At which point she regains her senses, becomes aware of her nudity, and is clothed by a bystander.
In another version, from the Appadana, the Buddha says:
*Daughter, do not mourn, be confident, seek yourself.
Why do you grieve uselessly?
Neither children, nor a father, nor any relative are a shelter.
Relatives are no protection for one who is affected by death.*
The commentary adds a second verse:
*Knowing this matter, a wise person restrained by morality would quickly purify the path leading to nirvana.*
With these words of comfort and wisdom, Patakara requested ordination as an entering stream-seeker, or sotapanna.
Her practice advanced to bhikkhuni, or nun, and finally to arhat, one who has achieved salvation from all defilements.
This takes place many generations before Mahayana Buddhism's bodhisattva concept emerged.
There's a poem in the Theragata about Patakara's becoming an arhat and then her designation as a master of the basket of discipline.
Here's the story, followed by a contemporary poem based on that canonical text.
One day, while washing her feet, Patakara poured water out of her pot.
The water went a little way and stopped.
She poured it a second time and it went a little further.
The third time it went a little further again.
In this meditation she realized the three ages of life.
*Like the pouring of the water, some of these beings die in the first stage of life.
Those who go farther than that, like the second pouring of the water, die in middle age.
And those who go farther than that, like the third time I poured out the water, surely die in the last stage of life.*
The Buddha, sitting radiant in his perfume cottage, appeared and said:
*Better than not seeing the rise and fall of the five constituents of mind and body while living for a hundred years, is seeing the rise and fall for even a day or even a moment.*
And then he spoke this verse:
*And should one live one hundred years not seeing the rise and demise, better still is one day of seeing the rise and demise.*
And here's the poem from the Theragata, sections 112 through 116.
*Young Brahmins plow fields, sow seeds, nourish their wives and children, get wealthy.
Why can't I find peace?
I'm virtuous, comply with the teacher, not lazy or puffed up.
One day washing my feet, I watched the water as it trickled down the slope.
I fixed my mind the way you'd train a thoroughbred horse.*
*Later, taking my lamp, I entered my cell, sat on my bed and watched the flame.
I extinguished the wick with a needle.
The release of my mind is like the quenching of the lamp.
Oh, the nirvana of this little lamp.*

It is said that her interest in the rules of conduct was attributed to her reflections on being a woman who refused to abide by the rules of society, to one who later became the most diligent and disciplined.

While sitting in [unclear: "Jeddah Woods"] and placing the nuns successively in their respective positions, the Buddha placed Patakara in the foremost position of those who bore the discipline in mind.
Over time, Patakara developed a huge following of over 500 disciples, some of whose texts are also included in Theragata.

So our story begins with a beautiful, rich woman who had everything except her personal freedom, which she pursues with her servant-lover contrary to her caste and all social norms, and then horribly suffers the loss of all she loves, including her own mental stability.
The Buddha listens to her story with understanding of her karmic past and of her current profound depression and madness.
He is there to listen and accept, to respond in that moment with the appropriate expedient means.
In this case, a few guiding words.
The Buddha listened and he responded, probably with a few more words than are carried forward in tradition.
Most importantly, he listened, he heard, and he spoke a truth that penetrated Patakara's darkness and opened the path to light and peace.
If we step back from this extreme drama, we can ask ourselves: How do we listen to the pain and suffering of others in and of the world we encounter each moment?
How and when do we respond?
How do we understand the situation right before our eyes?
How do we accept the impermanence of our lives, of all life, and embrace its continuity, transformation, and joy?
How do we accept and embrace the inevitable reality of death in this ever-transforming body?
One consequence of facing death is a release from petty concerns and frivolities.
What is truly important?
The reality of this moment, its profundity and transience, is a continuing wake-up call to see the rise and fall of each moment without holding on, without attachment.
To take the next breath and to keep our hearts open and joyful.
Let me close with a commentary on verses 288 and 289 of the Dhammapada, Buddha's words to Patakara about death and nirvana.
*All beings die.
Life ends in death.
Beings fare according to their deeds, experiencing the result of their meritorious and sinful deeds.
Those who do sinful deeds go to the woeful states, and those who do meritorious deeds attain blissful states.
Therefore, let one always do good deeds, which serve as a store for life elsewhere.
Meritorious deeds are great support to beings in the future world.*
So, let us go forward with Kisa Gotami and Patakara's open hearts and minds, filled with devotion and gratitude as we cherish all living beings.
Thank you for your attention.
So, do we have time to talk?
Sure, let's see.
Do we have a minute?
It's 9:40, I mean 8:40.
So, let's take about ten minutes and just pose a question to you, given these stories.
How does your practice aid you in finding detachment from grief and to helping find resilience from difficulties and tragedy?
How does your practice aid you in finding detachment from grief and resilience from difficulties and tragedy?

That leaves very little time, maybe groups of three?
Three, okay, three.
Groups of three.

Okay, groups of two, five minutes each.
That's fine.

I don't have a watch, so I can't tell you.
So, we have fifteen minutes to play around.
Let's help out, groups of three and five minutes each.
Okay.
Turn it off.
Thank you so much for all your help.
